title: An orchestrator that waits in background tasks works in turns no driver wraps, so a failure there is seen by nothing
foundBy: user report (host), from the operator postmortems of two campaigns of one profile that ran the same night, one orchestrator waiting in the foreground and one in background tasks
details:
**What happened.** Two campaigns of one profile ran on the same night. Both orchestrators were on the claude CLI, and they waited for their members in two different ways.

The first called `cs-campaign-member wait` in the foreground, each call blocking for about four minutes. Its whole mission ran as one turn that the host started, 3h13m long. The CLI's session record marks only its start and its end. A provider error in the middle of a response ended that turn, and the turn log classed it `capacity`. That half is now covered: see the note on SAC-054 dated today.

The second launched each `wait` as a background task of its CLI and ended its turn. The turn the host started ended after 13 minutes with exit 0. The orchestrator then ran 22 more turns, each started by its CLI when a background wait finished. It dispatched, accepted and merged for 3h19m, and every look at `cs-campaign observe <campaign>` read:

```
orchestrator  node-stopped  m1  0 cont, 0 restarts · continue next · last turn ended 3h ago, exit 0 · session record changed 16s ago
```

**Why.** A turn driver wraps only what the host started, and only the driver writes the turn log, `~/.cs-turns/<cli>.log`. SAC-036 made `Compute` read `node-working` while the agent says it is `busy`, which sees a self-started turn while it runs. Between turns this orchestrator is idle, waiting on its background task. Most looks therefore find no driver, an idle agent, and a turn log whose newest line is the mission turn's clean exit. `Compute` in `internal/protocol/state.go` then falls through to `node-stopped · continue next`. The record age beside it is evidence only, and MANUAL.md says it "changes no state and no ladder move".

**Why it matters.** A provider error in any of those self-started turns is written to no turn log. It carries no class, trips no `providerWaitSeconds` bound and derives no resume, so `cs-campaign resume` would refuse it as a continue that spends a rung. The line reads the same whether the orchestrator is waiting on a background task or has died, until a person notices the record age growing. A person who acts on `continue next` in the meantime spends a rung on an orchestrator that is working.

**No document says which waiting mode is supported.** PROTOCOL.md section 8 draws the orchestrator as "one long turn" that calls a blocking wait. The orientation and the mission dispatch say only "Never end your turn without either calling `wait` or replying". A wait launched in the background and followed by the end of the turn obeys that sentence. SPEC.md R125 already records a model that "backgrounded a poller and ended its turn".

**How to reproduce.** Create a campaign with a claude orchestrator whose brief tells it to run `cs-campaign-member wait` as a background task and then end its turn. After its first dispatch, run `cs-campaign observe <campaign>` every few minutes. The orchestrator reads `node-stopped · continue next` while its branch and its claimed log keep moving. Arm a provider error on one of its later turns, as the claude fault scenario does. The turn log gains no line, and `cs-campaign resume <campaign>` refuses. The last two steps are read from the code and have not been run.

**What would help.** Three changes, and they compose:

1. Read the turns no driver wrapped from the session record. The CLI records every turn's end and any provider error there, whoever started the turn. A turn-log line derived from it would give those turns a class, the bound and a resume.
2. Let a stopped orchestrator's record age decide a state. SAC-036 rejected the record as a liveness measure because a node blocked in one long tool call writes nothing. That objection does not arise here, since this rule applies only with no driver alive and an agent that is not busy. A record that keeps changing means working, and one that has been still for longer than the seat's `stallSeconds` means stopped.
3. Say which mode the harness supports. If only the foreground is supported, the orientation and the mission dispatch should say to call `wait` there and never as a background task. `observe` should then say when the orchestrator's turns come from nothing the host started.

notes.text:
Decided, by the reporter, how to fix this. Background waiting is made safe, and foreground waiting becomes the documented style. Supporting background waiting fully (building turn ends from the session record for turns no driver wrapped) is left for later, and refusing a backgrounded `wait` is dropped, because telling that a command runs as a background task needs knowledge of each agent family and the harness is family-neutral.

**R64 is amended, not bypassed.** It says a record's age must not decide a state, because slow silent work (a long model call, a long tool call) also leaves the record unchanged. The new rule reads the age only when two liveness facts already agree that nothing is running: an orchestrator whose turn driver is absent, whose agent answers `idle` (not `busy`) to its family's `--state`, and whose session record has not changed for longer than one `wait` chunk can block (R126's bound) plus a margin, is `node-stuck`, with a reason that says so. A thinking model answers `busy` and is never caught. A background `wait` always wakes the agent within one chunk, so idle past that bound means the wake never came. Every input is one every family already provides: the driver in the process table, `--state`, the record age, the chunk bound.

**Foreground waiting is the documented style.** The orientation, the mission dispatch and the playbook say to call `wait` in the foreground, where a provider error ends a turn the driver wraps and `resume` recovers it (SAC-054).

**Tests.** `Compute` cases: idle with a stale record past the bound goes `node-stuck`; busy with the same stale record stays `node-working` (R64's case); idle within the bound stays `node-stopped`. A fault scenario for the smoke tier in which the orchestrator waits in the background and its wake never comes. The document-claim tests hold SPEC, MANUAL and PLAYBOOK to the amended rule.
